opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a balance I think about a lot, and honestly it's shifted over the years. Early on, when I was doing my PhD and in the first few years at DeepMind, I read a lot. I'd go through arXiv pretty much daily, and that was really valuable for building up intuition about what had been tried and what the landscape looked like.

These days I'd say the ratio has tilted much more toward working on ideas with the team. Partly that's just the nature of the role, but partly it's a deliberate choice. At the frontier, a lot of the most important things you learn come from your own experiments at scale, and those results often aren't in the published literature, either because other labs aren't publishing them or because the questions are specific to the setup you have. So the marginal value of reading every paper goes down a bit, and the marginal value of running a really clean experiment and actually understanding the result goes up.

That said, I don't think you can ever drop reading entirely. I try to be quite selective: I'll skim a lot of titles and abstracts, and then go deep on a small number of papers that seem to be either really surprising or that touch directly on something we're struggling with. And I lean a lot on the people around me. If you've got a team of strong researchers who are each reading in their own areas, the useful ideas tend to bubble up in conversation. Someone will say, "Oh, there was this paper that tried exactly that, and here's what went wrong." That kind of distributed reading is far more efficient than one person trying to keep up with everything.

The other thing I'd say is that there's a real risk in reading too much before you try something. You can talk yourself out of an idea because some paper reported a negative result, when actually their setup was different or they didn't push it far enough. Some of the most interesting progress comes from people who were maybe a little naive and just tried the thing properly. So I try to keep some space for that: form your own hypothesis, run the experiment, and then go back to the literature to contextualize what you found.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts his earlier PhD and early-career reading with his current focus on team ideas, but does not say this reflects a shift toward directing research.

r002.rationale: It says important learning comes from the team’s own experiments because results and setup-specific questions often are not covered in published literature.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the balance has shifted a lot over the course of my career, and probably in the opposite direction from what people might expect.

Early on, I read a huge amount. When I was at DeepMind working on memory and long-context models, I felt like I needed to know everything that had been published on attention, on external memory, on compression, because the field was small enough that you actually could. And that was useful. A lot of the ideas we built on came from reading things carefully and noticing where the assumptions didn't quite hold.

But at some point the volume of papers crossed a threshold where reading comprehensively just isn't possible anymore, and I also started noticing that a lot of what gets published is lagging what's actually working inside labs by a fair margin. So now I'd say I spend much less time reading end to end. I skim a lot. I rely on people on the team who have a particular nose for a subfield to surface the two or three things a month that genuinely matter. And I try to keep a short list of questions I actually care about, so that when I do read something, it's in service of answering one of those rather than just keeping up.

The bigger allocation of my time now goes to the pursuing side, but with a caveat. I think the most valuable thing I can do with a team isn't to generate the ideas myself, it's to be the person who's willing to look at an experiment that's giving a confusing result and say, let's not move on yet, let's actually understand this. A surprising number of the things that have worked for us came from someone staring at a loss curve or an eval that didn't make sense and refusing to explain it away.

So if I had to put rough numbers on it, maybe a day a week on reading and talking to people outside the immediate team, and the rest on the work itself. But I'd stress that the reading is most useful when it's adversarial, when you're reading something because you suspect it's wrong, or because it conflicts with a result you have. Reading to confirm what you already believe is close to a waste of time, and I think a lot of people, myself included at points, have fallen into that.

r001.rationale: The response says the balance shifted over his career and describes a team-focused role now, but it does not connect reduced reading to a shift from junior researcher to directing research.

r002.rationale: It attributes less reading to the volume of papers and published work lagging what labs are doing, but does not say the team’s problems lack published solutions.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a balance, and it shifts depending on what we’re working on. Reading is incredibly valuable because you don’t want to spend months rediscovering something that somebody’s already figured out. But there’s also a failure mode where you spend all your time following other people’s framing of the problems, and you never give your own ideas enough space to develop.

So I tend to prefer having a concrete question in mind. We’re trying to understand something, we have a hypothesis, and then reading becomes much more directed: what have people tried, what evidence is there, and what might we be missing? And then you go back and run experiments. Often the result of an experiment makes a paper much more useful, because suddenly you understand why a particular detail matters.

I wouldn’t think of it as a fixed percentage so much as a feedback loop. You want enough awareness of the literature to be informed, but enough time working through things with the team to form an independent view.

r001.rationale: It discusses balancing reading with team work but does not link reduced reading to a career shift from junior researcher toward directing research.

r002.rationale: It says reading can prevent rediscovering existing work, but does not explain that less reading is due to the team’s problems lacking published solutions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a balance between staying informed and giving yourself enough space to develop an independent view. Reading papers can be incredibly useful, especially when you have a specific question. But there’s an almost unlimited amount you could read, and it’s easy to confuse keeping up with making progress.

So I tend to think in terms of what we’re trying to understand as a team. What’s the key uncertainty? What experiment would change our minds? Then reading becomes more directed: you look for work that helps you answer that question, rather than trying to absorb everything that’s coming out.

And I think you need some uninterrupted time to pursue an idea before judging it against the literature again. Otherwise, you can end up following everyone else’s framing. The useful loop is to read, form your own hypothesis, test it, and then go back to the literature with a better understanding of what matters.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses balancing reading with independent thinking but does not connect reduced reading to a shift from junior researcher to research director.

r002.rationale: It says reading should target team uncertainties, but does not say he reads less because the team’s problems lack published solutions.
